content:

content:
City of Malibu:

"After the Palisades and Franklin Fires, the City of Malibu is committed to making the rebuild process faster, clearer, and easier so homeowners can rebuild as quickly and safely as possible. The Community Development Department led by Director Yolanda Bundy has been holding working meetings with local building professionals and homeowners to gather feedback and identify ways to streamline the process. The City is continuing the meeting series with Design Professionals Meetings October 2, December 3, and November 13; and Fire Rebuild Community Sessions October 15, November 18, December 11, and January 14. All of the meeting details will be posted on the Rebuild website. "

https://maliburebuilds.org/Events/#Calendar

content:
As a trained firefighter I'm astounded/horrified at the number of reporters not wearing masks while reporting on the fires in LA.

A good story isn't worth sacrificing your life and health to hydrocarbons and burning plastic. The average home in 2025 is so toxic while burning that it's hard to watch; far more toxic than homes historically have ever been throughout history. This is something they drilled into us deeply while training.

The cause and effect can be long term and utterly devastating. A mask is gonna save your life in the coming years, be it pandemic or flames.

Wear a mask, shower often. Wash your hands before you eat. A lot of firefighters died before we figured out those basics.

PS- if you have a paint respirator with VOC cartridges even better.

#maskUp #palisades #LA #fire #journalism #staySafeLA

content:
@RobotDiver
One who waited much too long to mask up was gasping and wheezing her way through interviews on the burning streets this morning 🙄

@me_valentijn

Heartbreaking
@RobotDiver Thanks. All stuff I hadn't known.
@RobotDiver mask like FFP3 already OK or does have to me some better class? Are we talking about small particles of gas like substances?

@utzer

Better is always better, but an n95 is a good start. I think an FFP3 is the equivalent of an n99 in Canada.

@utzer

Paint respirators with replaceable cartridges are fantastic

@utzer
FFP3 is the bare minimum, but particulates are only part of the concern with building fires. You really want something that'll deal with toxic gasses as well - something like an ABEK P3 filter on a full mask would probably be ideal, unless you're walking right into a burning building (SCBA is the only way to go for that). However, using what you have or can easily get is definitely better than not using any filters at all.
@RobotDiver

@RobotDiver
Particulate masks like N95 and P100 only provide limited protection against toxins from fire.

The most seriously toxic parts of the smoke are gases and go straight through masks, as does much of the smoke itself.

This is why firefighters use breathing apparatus with full face masks and bottled air.

Organic solvent respirator masks are an in-between solution and have a mass of charcoal filtering which absorbs more of the toxic gases and smoke.

...

@RobotDiver

Yes, wear a mask when that's the best you have, but avoid all exposure to the smoke and fumes from fires.

@zl2tod 💯

A paint respirator with VOC cartridges are ideal, but not available to everyone. Any mitigation is better than none.
@zl2tod @RobotDiver 3M recommendations: https://web.archive.org/web/20221203020458/https://multimedia.3m.com/mws/media/1722719O/wildfire-ppe-suggested-respiratory-protection.pdf

@RobotDiver my cousin died last friday, same first and middle name as me "Aaron Christopher Johnston", from non-Hodgkins lymphoma from a US Marine Corps tour during iraq surge in 2006-2008 where there was burn pits, he was subjected to heavy metal and burning pit contaminents which caused fatal cancer. He was 5 years younger than me.

@ludiusvox I'm so sorry to hear that. It's part of why i joined the Canadian coast guard instead of becoming a career fire fighter in the long run. They were very open about the long term dangers of exposure. It's why i have unbelievable respect for anyone who does fire fighting work. It's a sacrifice on all levels.
@RobotDiver I’m no fire fighter but I looked like Anderson Cooper was way,way too close today.

@RobotDiver

It is nuts that these many of these reporters aren't wearing masks. What are they thinking???

@CindyWeinstein @RobotDiver
I guess the same reason a lot of main characters on TV & film run around with their heads unprotected while their minions or side kicks are properly covered - seeing the face makes a human connection. That principal combined with ignorance of the risks, I suppose.

@econads @RobotDiver

Could be but of course not covering their faces creates more ignorance. It's an opportunity for the media person to educate those watching.
@CindyWeinstein @RobotDiver yeah for sure

@RobotDiver A lot of these reporters are talking about their own houses in the Palisades and Pasadena. They're also dumb enough to call firefighting "a firefight." If I had perfect teeth and an 88 IQ I'd huff burning plastic once every five years in exchange for an 8 million dollar house.

@alrs

Man, they must pay better than in Canada then. I know two news reporters and they both rent.

@RobotDiver @alrs

LA local news is a big time gig.

@RobotDiver about twenty years ago i wound up stuck in traffic near a single house fire. That was really terrible and we were a few blocks away. I can't imagine how bad it would be up close.

Also, those paint resporators are great! They're much more comfortable than a disposable mask. I did learn the hard way that they need to be wiped out after use or they get kind of yucky inside.

@RobotDiver @ireneista Past a certain point isn't the gaseous portion of the byproducts enough to doom one to chronic issues despite a particle-filter respirator?

My feeling is that anything short of chemical filters is reporters being reckless.

@lispi314 this is the second time you've responded to something we reshared to, effectively, tell people to despair about masks on the false theory that masks are useless, which is not an empowering thing to do even though it's framed as concern

we do not appreciate it

@lispi314 if this is going to be a pattern, we may eventually need to block you so that you can no longer use our reshares as a means of discovering threads to use in spreading what amount to anti-mask talking points. we don't know whether that is your intent, but it is what you are doing. we don't want to block you, but if you test us, we will.
@lispi314 we view you as a friend, but we recognize that we and you have very different communication styles. we are being blunt in order to make sure we don't miscommunicate.
@lispi314 if you want to talk about your complaints around masks in your own space, feel free. we object to being an intermediary who helps you to reach a larger audience with this stuff.
@lispi314 thanks for understanding.
@ireneista I had not intended this aspect, apologies for that.
@lispi314 thank you

@ireneista I'm not arguing that particle filter masks (respirators) are ineffective against biohazards. They are most certainly effective.

The fact is that this is also a chemical hazard and people should make sure to use the appropriate filters for it too.

Most reusable/elastomeric respirators that aren't of the absolute cheapest kind allow for various kinds of filter cartridges including ones for chemical safety. Reporters should be leading by example, since people will see them.

Filtering out the ash and particles still necessarily helps, but why not do even better when it's possible?

@lispi314 we agree that people who have the time and resources to take more robust precautions, should strongly consider doing so. however, the effect of raising the topic in the way you did is to discourage people, not encourage them, by characterizing any realistic effort as useless.

@lispi314 we realize that we normally are very willing to help you understand the implications of the thing you say, which very frequently seem as if they're coming from some sort of alternate reality. we're not up for doing that right now, we're just setting a boundary. if you contemplate this topic on your own and come back to us with any questions you still have, we're willing to discuss it some other time.
@ireneista Alright, noted.
@lispi314 thanks 💜

@ireneista @lispi314

I'm gonna butt in as a stranger and say thank you both so much for practicing clear communication and de-escalation / conflict resolution strats so openly. It's really nice to see, especially these days.

</thankful rubber-necking,I guess?>
@MxVerda we're glad it came off that way, we worried about it, it's more intense than we usually are

@Beachbum

It's sadly common

The JPL Emergency Page at https://emergency.jpl.nasa.gov/ has additional info -

- JPL will remain closed until Monday, Jan 13
- All personnel are under mandatory telework with no Lab access except for designated personnel
- JPL facilities, labs and hardware are secured and protected.
- Deep Space Network (DSN) operations have been moved offsite to a back-up operations center.

3/n

The Wildland Fire Potential Index (WFPI) from the USGS forecasts the risk for large fire activity across the U.S.

It is a unit-less number that ranges from 0 to 150 and relates to vegetation flammability. It describes the ratio of live to dead fuel and includes variables for wind speed, dry bulb temperature, and rainfall.

The wildfires in the L.A. area are not unexpected. The WFPI values around L.A. are mostly in the red zone. The Santa Ana winds spread the fire.

https://firedanger.cr.usgs.gov/viewer/index.html
4/n

The wildfire situation around JPL looks very dire. This is a map of the wildfire in the area over the past 12 hours from the NASA FIRMS system. Note that there are a lot of residential areas underneath that red blob.

We are certainly not prepared for natural disasters like this. We will be even less so after the new fossil-fueled, ravenous billionaire infused, sociopathic administration takes over.

https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/map/#m:advanced;d:2025-01-08%2014:10..2025-01-09%2002:10;l:fires_landsat_landsat,fires_modis_aqua,fires_modis_terra,fires_viirs_noaa20,fires_viirs_noaa21,fires_viirs_snpp,countries,earth;@-118.13,34.20,12.98z

But I think people need to glimpse these to get a sense of the destruction and the human toll caused by these disasters, even though we may not have personally experienced them (yet). And the fact that these situations will only get worse unless we stop the billionaire class and the far-right from ravaging our dear earth.

This is CNN's Anderson Cooper reporting on the horrific scenes in the Altadena neighborhood east of JPL.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L45PLpkfvgM

"The inexpensive labor of incarcerated firefighters is a critical part of CA’s plan to get through wildfire season, which has become, as a symptom of the climate crisis, an almost year-round concern.

Roughly 27% of the state’s firefighters were incarcerated in 2018 and 2019, earning mere dollars a day while free firefighters make an average $41.76 an hour."
😠

Here are devastating before-and-after satellite images from Maxar Technologies of a few blocks in Altaneda in visible light.

Now let's imagine what it looks and feels like at street level.
Imagine households with young children, infants, the elderly, the disabled.
Houses full of memories. All gone.

These are horrific tragedies, made all the worse by Climate Change and an unholy union of billionaires and a political party that seem hell bent on making this worse.

https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-01-08/shocking-before-and-after-satellite-images-show-destruction-of-malibu-and-altadena-neighborhoods
9/n

The Eaton wildfire has reached the edge of the Mount Wilson Observatory area, north of Altadena 🙁

Power is out. The observatory website is down.

The site also hosts many towers for TV and radio transmission.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Spo1lkghEY8

The map below shows the approx. location of the video camera at Mt. Wilson which is webcasting the video in the previous post. The camera is located high on a tower near the area with many TV towers. The smoke and small fires are located on the steep rightward slope.

The Mount Wilson observatory is further east and at a higher elevation.

The various aircraft supporting the fight against wildfires in CA include two "Super Scooper" Canadair CL-415 aircraft lent by Canada.

The CL-415 can scoop up to 6,140 L of water from a lake or ocean, optionally mix it with a chemical foam, and drop it on a fire without having to return to base to refill its tanks.

The CL-415 needs a 12-second 410-metre-long run at 70 knots to scoop up the water and it requires considerable skill to fly.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fuLk5hXMRZY
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadair_CL-415

dat satellite tech
@AkaSci seriously can't get over the resolution of this IR data. you could see if someone's backyard BBQ was going

@spacegeck
I suspect Maxar has even better resolution images than that for their paying customers.

Their newer satellites achieve 30-cm raw resolution. They also mention "derived 15-cm high-definition (HD) imagery."

You probably could apply your magic to bring out additional details.

https://www.maxar.com/press-releases/maxar-intelligence-releases-first-images-from-its-next-generation-worldview-legion-satellites

@AkaSci Not sure what they mean by derived, but presumably 30 cm raw visible light resolution is a bit lower in the infrared, maybe more like 40-60cm, but still obvious enough to see if someone's BBQ is flaring up... I put the lower limit at flaming bag of poop, if it gets hot enough

@spacegeck
Question - If you had multiple images of a scene, taken at different times at slightly different spatial offsets and angles (dithering), could they be processed to "derive" a higher effective resolution image?

@AkaSci @spacegeck Yes. Astrophotographers regularly do sth similar called “drizzling”, especially for planetary photography which is usually done by taking raw video to get 1000s of shots, the best of which are selected and combined (“stacked”). Drizzling is one technique in there to increase effective resolution.
See https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drizzle_(image_processing)
@databu @AkaSci I'm not sure how that would work with something as dynamic as a scene on earth, though. Drizzling is the first thing that came to mind, but "derived" could mean anything these days.

@spacegeck @AkaSci is it really that much more dynamic when compared to planetary images which are affected by seeing? I’m not an expert in the internals of drizzle algorithms, but they must be able to cope with quite some variance?

@databu @AkaSci for planetary images and all the seeing problems introduced by the atmosphere they are using something called "lucky" imaging. Taking a whole bunch of them (thousands) and then sifting through all of them for the best, least distorted ones to combine into a final image. I'm not really sure that Wikipedia article is really correct.... but maybe I'm the wrong one! I've only messed with drizzling a handful of times. I always assumed it needed four virtually pristine images with a subpixel shift... not, say, something with people walking around, or perspective changes from a satellite orbiting. Then again the satellite may actually take exposures that quickly.

@spacegeck @AkaSci as far as I know, lucky imaging is actually a simplified name for a multi-stage process: 1. A subset of best-quality images (there might not actually be any really pristine ones, depending on the conditions), and 2. Stacking algorithms which reject individual pixels from individual selected images based on statistical measurements. This might catch walking people etc.
@spacegeck @AkaSci But I’m not sure how drizzle is implemented within that flow, so it might or might not apply in this case.

@spacegeck @databu @AkaSci It's definitely a machine learning method. Not sure how I feel about it being applied to analytical data...
https://blog.maxar.com/earth-intelligence/2020/hd-satellite-imagery-and-machine-learning-more-accurately-detect-and-locate-features-of-interest-with-greater-consistency?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=51-cm-hd

@spacegeck @AkaSci Or, you know, the tailpipe of a T-90 tank.

Commercial imagery is very much a side business for Maxar.
@simonbp @AkaSci I was trying to avoid realistic topics. 😔

@simonbp @spacegeck
Doesn't the NRO have higher resolution satellites, with higher number of wavelengths/bands as well as SAR?

Although the article below mentions NRO's contracts with Maxar and other imaging satellite companies.

https://euro-sd.com/2024/07/articles/39425/the-black-world-of-us-spy-satellites/

@AkaSci @simonbp @spacegeck The NRO buys a lot of data (millions of dollars per year) from commercial satellites, including Maxar optical data and SAR from Capella, Umbra, and ICEYE. They like to get data that is unclassified and can easily be shared with allies, even if they have better classified images.

@spacegeck @EricFielding
Here is some additional zoomable hi-res imagery of the fire-affected areas in LA from the National Geodetic Survey.

Can't tell which satellites and other assets they use to generate these maps.

Actually they do mention MAXAR at the bottom right corner of the map.

https://storms.ngs.noaa.gov/storms/2025_eri/index.html#17.61/34.188576/-118.131741
@AkaSci @spacegeck Yes, I have seen a Maxar very-high-resolution satellite image acquired on Jan. 10 in several viewers.

@AkaSci @spacegeck Thanks for the link to the NOAA viewer, it is much more informative with the streets labeled and other annotation. The Maxar images I saw before were hard to navigate. The data may be the same, but the NOAA viewer is much better.

@EricFielding @spacegeck
We can see how close to JPL the fires got. Most houses east of Lincoln Ave in the map look burned.
https://storms.ngs.noaa.gov/storms/2025_eri/index.html#15.41/34.198076/-118.163023

@AkaSci @spacegeck Yes, I believe the closest house that was completely destroyed was about 400 meters east of the East Gate of JPL (where the bridge crosses the Arroyo Seco river). The building where I work is another 400 meters further west.
@EricFielding @AkaSci @spacegeck 😱 ☹️

@AkaSci @EricFielding @spacegeck

That's the Arroyo Seco in between - as the name indicates, it is dry, and a good fire break.

@TMEubanks @AkaSci @spacegeck Yes, the Arroyo Seco is a good firebreak for slowly moving ground fires, but I am not sure it would have stopped the streams of burning embers that were blowing in the wind, if the fire had reached the last line of houses across from JPL.
@EricFielding @AkaSci @spacegeck Yes, but JPL is also a harder target - few trees, no significant wooden buildings, most flat fire-proof roofs, etc.

@TMEubanks @EricFielding @spacegeck
Glad you did not get to test these features against a real firestorm.

@AkaSci @TMEubanks @spacegeck Yes, JPL has been hardened against fire in many ways, but we had previously expected the fire to approach from the north through the mountains. A previous fire, the 2009 Station Fire got within 300 meters of JPL northern edge, but there was no wind that day. The winds last week were unusually strong and damaged several buildings at JPL without the fire reaching the campus.

@AkaSci @TMEubanks @spacegeck The area near the East Gate is the oldest part of JPL and includes Building 11 that was built around 1940, long before there were advanced fire-resistant building designs. I am sure it has been upgraded since it was built but I bet it has a wood frame inside.
@EricFielding @AkaSci @spacegeck Yes, when I was at JPL that part of the Lab had older "temporary" buildings made of wood, but with metal roofs.
@AkaSci OMFG 💔

content:
Eaton Canyon fire: A second wind-whipped wildfire is burning out of control in the Los Angeles area

A fast-moving wildfire broke out Tuesday (January 7, 2025) in the inland foothills northeast of Los Angeles hours after another blaze tore through the city’s Pacific Palisades neighbourhood along the coast, destroying many homes and prompting evacuation orders for tens of thousands.

The Eaton fire in Altadena started near a nature preserve just before 6:30 p.m. The flames spread so rapidly that staff at a senior care centre had to push dozens of residents in wheelchairs and hospital beds down the street to a parking lot where they waited in their bedclothes for ambulances and other vehicles to take them to safety.

To the west, the Pacific Palisades fire that started on Tuesday (Jan. 7) morning burned out of control into the night.

A firefighter works to extinguish flames as the Eaton Fire burns in Pasadena, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

The Los Angeles Fire Department put out a plea for off-duty firefighters to help fight the flames that were being pushed by winds topping 60 mph (97 kph) in some places and creating chaotic scenes as residents fled.

Thousands asked to evacuate as a wildfire devours homes, buildings in Los Angeles suburb

Over 30,000 people have been ordered to evacuate their homes in a Los Angeles suburb on January 7, 2025, as a wildfire leveled multiple homes, and devoured buildings even as strong winds tore through the region.
| Video Credit:
The Hindu

It was too windy for firefighting aircraft to fly, hampering the fight.

The Pacific Palisades fire swept through a Los Angeles hillside dotted with celebrity residences Tuesday (Jan. 7), burning homes and prompting evacuation orders. In the frantic haste to get to safety, roadways were clogged and scores of people abandoned their vehicles and fled on foot, some toting suitcases.

A firetruck drives past flames along the Pacific Coast Highway, as a wildfire burns in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

The traffic jam on Palisades Drive prevented emergency vehicles from getting through and a bulldozer was brought in to push the abandoned cars to the side and create a path, according to the LA Fire Department.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who was in Southern California to attend the naming of a national monument by President Joe Biden, made a detour to the canyon to see “firsthand the impact of these swirling winds and the embers,” and he said he found “not a few — many structures already destroyed.”

Officials did not give an exact number of structures damaged or destroyed in the Pacific Palisades wildfire, but they said about 30,000 residents were under evacuation orders and more than 13,000 structures were under threat.

Sparks fly as the Eaton Fire burns in Pasadena, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

And the worst could be yet to come. The blaze began around 10:30 a.m., shortly after the start of a Santa Ana windstorm that the National Weather service warned could be “life threatening” and the strongest to hit Southern California in more than a decade. The exact cause of the fire was unknown and no injuries had been reported, officials said.

Only about 25 miles (about 40 kilometres) northeast in Altadena, the Eaton fire was burning.

The winds were expected to increase overnight and continue for days, producing isolated gusts that could top 100 mph (160 kph) in mountains and foothills — including in areas that haven’t seen substantial rain in months.

Flames rise from homes along the Pacific Coast Highway towards Malibu as a wildfire burns in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

“By no stretch of the imagination are we out of the woods,” Mr. Newsom warned residents, saying the worst of the winds are expected between 10 p.m. on Tuesday (Jan. 7) and 5 a.m. Wednesday (Jan. 8). He declared a state of emergency on Tuesday (Jan. 7).

As of Tuesday (Jan. 7) evening, 28,300 households were without power due to the strong winds, according to the mayor’s office. About 15,000 utility customers in Southern California had their power shut off to reduce the risk of equipment sparking a blaze. A half a million customers total were at risk of losing power preemptively.

The Pacific Palisades fire quickly consumed about 4.6 square miles (11.6 square kilometres) of land in the Pacific Palisades neighbourhood in western Los Angeles, sending up a dramatic plume of smoke visible across the city. Residents in Venice Beach, some 6 miles (10 kilometres) away, reported seeing the flames. It was one of several blazes across the area.

A building burns during the Palisades Fire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

Sections of Interstate 10 and the scenic Pacific Coast Highway were closed to all non-essential traffic to aid in evacuation efforts. But other roads were blocked. Some residents jumped out of their vehicles to get out of danger and waited to be picked up.

Resident Kelsey Trainor said the only road in and out of her neighbourhood was completely blocked. Ash fell all around them while fires burned on both sides of the road.

“We looked across and the fire had jumped from one side of the road to the other side of the road,” Ms. Trainor said. “People were getting out of the cars with their dogs and babies and bags, they were crying and screaming. The road was just blocked, like full-on blocked for an hour.”

An Associated Press video journalist saw a roof and chimney of one home in flames and another residence where the walls were burning. The Pacific Palisades neighbourhood, which borders Malibu about 20 miles (32 kilometers) west of downtown LA, includes hillside streets of tightly packed homes along winding roads nestled against the Santa Monica Mountains and stretches down to beaches along the Pacific Ocean.

An AP photographer saw multi-million dollar mansions on fire as helicopters overhead dropped water loads. Roads were clogged in both directions as evacuees fled down toward the Pacific Coast Highway while others begged for rides back up to their homes to rescue pets. Two of the homes on fire were inside exclusive gated communities.

A building burns during the Palisades Fire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

Long-time Palisades resident Will Adams said he immediately went to pick his two kids up from St. Matthews Parish School when he heard the fire was nearby. Meanwhile, he said embers flew into his wife’s car as she tried to evacuate.

“She vacated her car and left it running,” Mr. Adams said. She and many other residents walked down toward the ocean until it was safe.

Mr. Adams said he had never witnessed anything like this in the 56 years he’s lived there. He watched as the sky turned brown and then black as homes started burning. He could hear loud popping and bangs “like small explosions,” which he said he believes were the transformers exploding.

“It is crazy, it’s everywhere, in all the nooks and crannies of the Palisades. One home’s safe, the other one’s up in flames,” Mr. Adams said.

Actor James Woods posted footage of flames burning through bushes and past palm trees on a hill near his home. The towering orange flames billowed among the landscaped yards between the homes.

A woman waters the area in front of her house before leaving following an evacuation order, as a wildfire burns in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, in Santa Monica, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

“Standing in my driveway, getting ready to evacuate,” Mr. Woods said in the short video on X.

Actor Steve Guttenberg, who lives in the Pacific Palisades, urged people who abandoned their cars to leave their keys behind so they could be moved to make way for fire trucks.

“This is not a parking lot,” Mr. Guttenberg told KTLA. “I have friends up there and they can’t evacuate. … I’m walking up there as far as I can moving cars.”

The erratic weather caused Mr. Biden to cancel plans to travel to inland Riverside County, where he was to announce the establishment of two new national monuments in the state. He remained in Los Angeles, where smoke was visible from his hotel, and was briefed on the wildfires. The Federal Emergency Management Agency approved a grant to help reimburse California for the firefighting cost.

Mr. Biden said in a statement that he and his team are communicating with state and local officials and he has offered “any federal assistance that is needed to help suppress the terrible Pacific Palisades fire”.

Vehicles drive along the Pacific Coast Highway, as a wildfire burns in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of west Los Angeles, California, U.S. on January 7, 2025.
| Photo Credit:
Reuters

Some trees and vegetation on the grounds of the Getty Villa were burned by late Tuesday (Jan. 7), but staff and the museum collection remain safe, Getty President Katherine Fleming said in a statement. The museum located on the eastern end of the Pacific Palisades is a separate campus of the world-famous Getty Museum that focuses on the art and culture of ancient Greece and Rome. The fire also burned Palisades Charter High School classrooms.

Film studios cancelled two movie premieres due to the fire and windy weather, and the Los Angeles Unified School District said it temporarily relocated students from three campuses in the Pacific Palisades area.

Recent dry winds, including the notorious Santa Anas, have contributed to warmer-than-average temperatures in Southern California, where there’s been very little rain so far this season. Southern California hasn’t seen more than 0.1 inches (0.25 centimetres) of rain since early May.

Published – January 08, 2025 12:09 pm IST

#California: ‘Seeking seed donations': The #Altadena #SeedLibrary looks ahead to #regrowth

Story by Alysia Gray Painter, January 13, 2025

"Following the Jan. 7 fire that swept through the city, growers and gardening groups are beginning to think about what is next, groups that include the Altadena Seed Library.

"This community is enormously dedicated to native plants, but also had many farmers and growers who lost generations of crops at community gardens and in backyards.

"#Wildlife coming down from the foothills has lost habitat and food. the air quality will be poor and temperatures will be higher without the lush greenery that protected us. not to mention the vast natural spaces that have burned and may benefit from help #reseeding.

"If you have seeds to spare — particularly native plants — please send a message. please share widely.

"Monetary donations are also requested, if you are able to donate.

"Seeds may be sent to 37 Auburn Ave. #8, Sierra Madre, CA 91024 c/o Altadena Seed Library."

content:
The California wildfires are an example of how quickly you can lose everything. People have lost homes, possessions and some have even lost their lives.

Disabled people are the canaries in the coal mine. Anything that can impact others will likely hit us faster and harder.

When you don’t have your physical health, your resilience is impaired. Surviving pandemics, wildfires and natural disasters becomes much harder.

Why aren’t we factored into emergency planning? If our needs were accounted for, everyone would be better off.

My latest article looks at how we can (and should) be saving the canaries. How deaths like those of Anthony and Justin Mitchell should never have happened.

If no one is coming to save us, we need to start discussing how we can save each other:

https://www.disabledginger.com/p/disabled-people-are-the-canaries

#wildfires #california #climatechange #eaton #altadena #palisades #disability #disabilityrights #ableism #emergencypreparedness #chronicillness

content:
@broadwaybabyto

There are professionals in the field who have the same lens as you. My daughter is the disability access and functional needs (dafn) planner for the office of emergency management in Philadelphia and is one of them.

It’s a relatively new niche in planning for emergency in all its forms and not all cities have a dafn specialist.

What has happened in LA is tragic on so many levels and is overwhelming to all involved.
@Kendal857 I’m so glad to hear there are people focusing on this and doing it for a living. We definitely need more of that!

@broadwaybabyto thank you for this! I recently read Sunaura Taylor's Disabled Ecologies and it also used the canary metaphor to great effect. no moral compasses intact on any of this. Climate injustice may be hard to consider but nobody emerges without moral injury
@marion_grau I’m not familiar with that but I will check it out! Sounds like something I would be interested in.

Sadly, my brother-in-law's house burned down in the #Eaton fire in #Altadena a week ago. He and his three boys are fine—which is really all that matters. However, they lost everything in the fire, and Eitan is trying to wade through both immediate and longer term needs that come with this new reality.

https://gofund.me/0cf40c99

I wanted to share the GoFundMe we set up to help him get through this time and the many costs that are not and will not be covered by insurance. Please feel free to share the link with anyone who is looking to support families who lost their homes in the #lafires, of which there are many.

Thank you. 🙏

content:
LA wildfires: death toll rises to 24 as winds threaten further destruction

More than 1,800 structures destroyed as #Eaton and #Palisades fires still less than 30% contained

Rich Thompson with the National Weather Service said the winds that had driven what he called
“very extreme fire behavior” last week were set to return but with lower intensity.

“Unfortunately, we’re still under a Santa Ana wind pattern and have expectation of moderate to strong winds through Wednesday …
with gusts anywhere from 35 to 55 miles per hour.”

The wind and dry conditions, he added, were “a recipe to produce some very critical fire weather conditions”.

LA fire chief Kristin Crowley said the impending winds demanded very close attention.

“This wind event is approaching us, and approaching us very, very quickly,” she said,
and sought to reassure Los Angelenos that city leaders were “ready for this next event”.

Crowley also asked the community to stay informed, “with trusted news and official updates”
and “be prepared to evacuate.”

“Follow all evacuation warnings and orders,
and without delay, and stay off the roadways and any impacted areas,” Crowley added.

content:
From chatting with people in re-insurance. Much of the house insurance you can get in CA seems poorly backed by re-insurance (same for Florida and flooding). I'm curious how this will all unfold. For one, as with natural disasters, many people will realize that they didn't read the fine print carefully enough.

#LAfire

https://www.windy.com/?hrrrConus,34.146,-118.467,11,m:eClacRJ - Both predicted and current wind data.

https://lafd.maps.arcgis.com/apps/Media/index.html?appid=0c7dd4c212b14e0d9de09c96773a8c6a - LAFD evac data. Not updated as often as https://protect.genasys.com/search but more official. Watch Duty feeds from both of these so that should show the needful anyway.

https://www.broadcastify.com/dashboards/?uuid=c44d6768-cdce-11ef-9e04-0e98d5b32039&t=6263 - Access to various FD and dispatch radios.

🧵 2/2 #LAFire

The list of resources I use for monitoring fires (such as the #LAFire right now):

https://app.watchduty.org/ - First stop, has live data reported from the ground.

https://www.fire.ca.gov/incidents/ - Calfire dashboard, updates slowly but high trust data. This is where official status updates are posted every few hours.

https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/usfs/map/ - FIRMS is a live feed of all space-based fire data. Because orbits this only updates every 2-6 hours but gives good data on burn areas.

🧵 1/2

I wish the news organizations covered government corruption, income inequality, the breakdown of our republic with as much tenaciousness and veracity as they are currently doing with the California wildfires.

#USA #LAFire

Джо Байден тоже утешил американцев, чьи дома сгорели из-за пожара: "Есть хорошая новость, я стал прадедушкой".
----
И смешно и грустно одновременно от таких городских чиновников. От их безалаберности страдают простые люди.

One thing I'm thinking about regarding the LA fires, is that there is enough destroyed where they could rebuild with more density, to close the housing gap. However, LA likely won't have the foresight to add density to housing in the areas (and maybe add buffer to the mountains). Which is unfortunate, as a place like the Pacific Palisades isn't terribly far from the planned Sepulveda Pass line or current Expo line.

@epp thank you!! thankfully my neighborhood was safe but i know people who lost everything, it’s very sad.

One small problem: This declaration doesn't exist. It's completely made up. content:
I have made a decision. I AM going to make my website a proper old school links page, of proper websites, made by proper people.

And I'm mortified by how few of those I visit these days (which is precisely why I need it of course).

I figure there's 3 main stages.

1. check out sites I used to like (& find people I've lost track with) & see what's still there & active from that group

2. check profiles of folk I chat to & follow on here for their websites

3. find new stuff

1 /n

Number 3 could be tricky.

Might need a hand with that.

Search engines are of limited use, too much slop, too many ads.

I need recommendations people!

Websites about music, art, politics, science, the absurd minutiae of everyday life. Anything & everything that makes us human.

Suggestions very welcome in reply.

Thanks :TotoroBambole:

2 /n

content: Even though we were still in relative safety, Kara and I made the decision to evacuate while it was easy to do so. Long ago, we had made preparations to aid us if we ever needed to leave, so we packed up and stayed in a hotel in Torrance for the night. We returned around 4pm the next day, and all is well. The air quality has been bad, but we are already set up with great filtration, thanks to COVID.

We are very fortunate, and we know people who were not. Our thoughts are with them. Thank you to everyone who has reached out.

A few things:

1. Thank you to our local officials and everyone who is risking their lives to fight these fires.

2. The Watch Duty app has proven incredibly valuable during this crisis, which is both a credit to the work of public officials and the Watch Duty team in disseminating the information.

3. There is a lot of bad info being spread online and bad actors (like Donald Trump and Elon Musk) personally attacking Californians and some of our officials. Large platforms divesting from community, moderation, trust, and safety work make these matters worse. For one, the bigoted attacks against LAFD Fire Chief Kristin Crowley are unacceptable.

4. I find it challenging to reconcile well wishes from folks who voted for Trump, knowing that he delayed wildfire aid to California in his first term until he was shown that enough Republicans lived here. Four months ago, Trump said that he would not provide California with the money needed to put out all fires. And here we are, 10 days away from his second term, where we will no doubt lose ground in the climate fight. As voters, your votes count for more than your words in this moment.

I'm glad you are both safe. Instead of BETTER community & moderation, trust and Safety the Trump fascist partnerships with Musk & Zuck, in a fact free platform, is more dangerous than people know.

Ok now there is a new fire in the Hollywood Hills in Hollywood. It is apparently spreading rapidly and a large chunk of the Hills is under mandatory Evac orders.

#SunsetFire

3 of my former apartment buildings are under Evac orders.

#SunsetFire

@ai6yr Broadcastify for #SunsetFire is reportedly LA County Fire V-4. Is this correct?

https://www.broadcastify.com/listen/feed/38654
Evacuations moving fast on Sunset Fire in the Hollywood Hills. Evacuate early, those are tight streets with a lot of dead ends. Evacs as of 1/8/25 1837PT #SunsetFire
@gmillikan Yes

Oh good. Now there's the #SunsetFire.

I see fire top the hills to the south, I'm packing up and catching a plane cross country.

@kirasha good luck.
Like the 2020s in general, it looks like it's going to get worse before it gets worse

#SunsetFire #CAwx

content:
@Dillerjohann @professor444

Only in "libtard" states like California! 😁

Daniel Swain @weatherwest clarified the interesting climate connection:
background to the fires are
*the 2 wettest, preceding years on record, which had plants grow enormously compared to what is normal in Southern #California;
*the hottest summer on record with its also record-high water hungry atmosphere;
*a bone-dry autumn and winter with almost no rain since October in the areas now on fire;
*unusual warmth these days with increased evaporation.

All of the above amassed bone-dry fuel load in the forest and grassy ecosystems and also of cultivated plants in the suburbs.
Without the extreme weather whiplash of extreme wetness followed by extreme heat=evaporation and extreme dryness,
ie, without climate change,
the fires wouldn't be so severe.

Additionally, a prolonged fire season due to #ClimateChange now easier meets with the recurring #SantaAna winter wind pattern.
A fire plus wind = billions of burning ambers are swirling around, entering houses through the tiniest cracks, and thus, burning structures from within. As well as spreading fires –  out of any attempt to control them.
Daniel showed these suburban snowstorm of burning ambers in his YT live streams yesterday. I had no idea this was a thing!

#EatonFire #PalisadesFire #HurstFire
#LidiaFire

@professor444

It can't be true that there is no climate change in America!

@anlomedad @professor444 @weatherwest

Rainfall amounts in previous years are irrelevant because they have long since run off. The soil cannot store it long-term, especially in mountainous regions. Stone does not store water, the extreme growth of plants is a result of increased nitrogen concentration in the air! Due to the massive combustion processes worldwide!

@Dillerjohann @professor444 @weatherwest

Record amount of rain in the 2 preceding years has let plants grow.

Now, this unusual amount of plant mass is bone dry, ready to receive the spark.
The fuel load is important in wildfires wrt heat creation, and via rising hot air, to fire propagation, ie the final area burned.

@Dillerjohann @professor444
Darfst Dich auch ruhig bedanken für die doppelten Erläuterungen. Manche brauchen halt Wiederholung, bis Fakten ihren Eigendünkel durchdringen können.

@anlomedad @professor444 @weatherwest

#PalisadesFire #EatonFire #HurstFire

3:19am. New Satellite heat detection data is now on the map. This data is not real time and locations are only approximate. Also, some of this data is likely ‘false positive’. This can be due to a combination of wind, heavy smoke with embers and the angle at which the satellite sees the ground. For more information open the map, click “Map tips” and read about MODIS/VIIRS.

#1 Rule - Never ignore an order to evacuate. The fire officials have information that you do not.

The brown arrow symbols are fire cameras. That layer is ‘on top’ and can be clicked. Follow the first link in the popup.
